Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata):	I would like to address a question
to the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) in regard to the so-called system of universal promotion for railway employees. I am told that there is an arrangement between the heads of the employees' brotherhoods to the effect that the system of universal promotion will be established in the near future. According to that system an employee who has seniority right in a railway region .will have that

seniority right all over that region. Accordingly a man from Riviere du Loup, in my constituency, will perhaps have to work on the Transcontenental railway if the other employees there are his juniors, and a man who works in New Brunswick may be sent to Prince Edivard Island or Nova Scotia or vice versa, for an indenfinite period of time. This would be very embarrassing to him, making it necessary to leave his family, and as everyone knows railway employees are not supposed to be Wandering Jews.
In that respect I would ask the Minister of Railways if it would not be proper, and if it is not the intention of the management of the Canadian National Railways, to ask the employees of every district to vote on that matter and decide among themselves what should be done in their own district.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING. (Minister of Railways and Canals):	I am informed,
Mr. Speaker, that these matters of seniority give considerable difficulty to the management of every railway in this country or in the United States. Up to the present it has been the policy of the management to endeavour, so far as possible, to have the men themselves, through their organizations, determine the broad general policy to be followed, provided that such a policy does not interfere with the proper management and conduct of the road, and does not add unduly to the cost of operation. With regard to the specific details to which my hon friend refers, there will, I am sure, be an excellent opportunity before the special committee which was appointed yesterday to go very thoroughly into details with the operating officers of the road, and I know that members whose constituents are affected will take advantage of that opportunity and get all detailed information regarding it.

Am I to understand that
the new proposal will not be enforced until the committee has reached a decision?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning I received from Winnipeg the following telegram which I wish to draw to the attention of the government: Yesterday the following notice appeared in the government employment office, one hundred miners (shooters and loaders) for shooting and loading coal. Must have experience and be able to qualify as miners. Single men preferred. Rates forty eight to fifty-five cents per ton according to height of seam. Applicants are expected to join union and be prepared to pay own transportation. Board eight dollars to nine dollars per week. Position permanent. Superintendents having applicants please communicate with superintendent of employment service of Canada, Sydney, Nova Scotia. We took this up with Bowman,-
Mr. Bowman, I might say, is the superintendent of employment service in the city of Winnipeg.
-who advised us to see Rigg.-
Mr. Rigg, Sir, is superintendent of the employment service for the Dominion of Canada, with offices in this city.
-We wired Rigg as follows: Employment office advertising for one hundred miners for Nova Scotia. Are you aware that the minors in Pictou county only working two days per week and hundreds idle? Cape Breton, Sydney Mines and Florence two days out of last two weeks. We protest government employment offices advertising for men under these conditions. Wire reply what you can do." We received the following wire in reply this morning: "Replying to your wire even date re miners for Nova Scotia. Coal production in Nova Scotia mines rapidly increasing and request for importation of European miners has been filed with the Department of Immigration. Our efforts directed towards meeting requirements from labour resident in Canada. We are advised that demand cannot be met in Maritime provinces. Signed R. A. Rigg." This is the lamest excuse ever heard. The fallowing are the wires received from New Glasgow, Sydney and Glace Bay. Sydney, Nova Scotia. All m;nes in Sydney Mines area have worked about one week since first of January. Glace Bay area almost as bad. When mines are operating they are overcrowded and contract men don't make three dollars a day.-

Customs tariff-7. Meats, fresh n.o.,p. per pound: British preferential tariff, 2 cents; Intermediate tariff 2£ cents; general tariff, 3£ cents.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yesterday my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) directed my attention to the question of the difference in the rate. I think he was following a copy of the consolidation of the customs tariff used in the department and sent out to the offices, but the half cent referred to in no way affects this.
That is what I wanted to know. The Australian rate remains at half a cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
And it is not in the special tariff, but it remains at half a cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Would the minister inform us on what basis this increase is made in connection with this matter. It is true that it may apply to the Australian treaty, but how does it come that the increase of half a cent a pound is made, and that the tariff is not put on an equality with the tariff of other countries in regard to this product?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The agreement with Australia was that we should give them a spread of three cents, and in transmitting the messages by cable a mistake was made, and this item is to corect that mistake, so that they will have a spread of three cents, instead of two and a half cents. It is an increase in the general tariff, raising the general tariff against the world, and automatically that gives Australia a spread of three cents. It does not change the Australian rate coming in, but gives them a half a cent more spread against the rest of the world.

The minister points out just exactly what happened with the Australian treaty. The real arrangement between Australia and Canada was that there should be a spread of three cents, and it was entirely in the hands of the government whether they would raise that rate in such a way as to protect the Canadian farmer,

or whether they would not. Perhaps my hon. friend would answer the question of the hon. member for South Oxford better if he would explain why he did not make the Australian rate two cents, the same as the British preference tariff, and the general rate five cents.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a question of policy.
The policy in the future is, I presume, to be dictated by the tariff board?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the Prime Minister
has already made that very clear to the House and the country. The tariff board is an inquiry board to examine into conditions, but the government of the day must accept the responsibility, and the 245 members elected to this House from the different constituencies in Canada will have the last-word to say as to what shall be the tariff policy of Canada,

We are now dealing with an item in the tariff-Under the arrangements made by the government with Australia-and a few weeks before the election the same privileges were extended to New Zealand-Australia maintains a tariff of five cents a pound against similar exports from this country going to Australia. That is the reason. I asked the minister if he would inform the House upon what principle or basis this reduction was founded? There surely must be some principle, because a change of three cents per pound against imports of fresh meats from Australia is going to result in tremendous imports into this country of such products as mutton and lamb from that country, and it is going to Ibe a great hardship on those engaged in producing similar meats in this country. So far neither the minister nor the government has informed the country why the reduction of two cents was made in regard to those commodities in those twi treaties. It is quite apparent that, as a result of the treaty, our favourable balance of trade with those two countries has already decreased very much indeed, away up in the millions, and this is another evidence of an attempt to sacrifice the interests of agriculture to obtain some other concessions from other countries, and while on the surface it may appear as some degree of relief, as a matter of fact it is not, because of the danger to which I have referred of large imports from those countries. Now our good neighbours to the south of us are continually exporting into this country, or our people are importing from that country, large quantities, particularly of pork products, under this item, and instead of having an increase of half a.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
cent a pound, I think the government w.ould be well advised to make that five cents a pound, and then have your tariff board inquire into the matter. It is surely a matter which should be remedied. It is absolutely unfair to those engaged in agriculture in this province that they should have to submit to conditions of that kind, because it affords a convenient channel for dumping to take place in Canada from the United States. It has happened in the past and is the practice to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I had better place on
record the real trade before any other hon. member speaks. My hon. friends opposite apparently change their policy every day. Heretofore they have been finding fault because of the importations from the United States and have said that we should increase duties against United States products and improve trade within the empire. That is exactly what we are doing under this legislation. We are increasing the rate against the United States and we are lowering the rate to the other British dominions where we have the preference. We.have no preference in the United States. Let us look into it and find out how the trade has been flowing in recent years, and how farm products have been coming into Canada. The statistics I have here are not quite up-to-date, because they are for the year ending March, 1925, but I imagine they are fairly correct for the other years. The total importations of fresh beef for the fiscal year 1925 were $39,638; of that $69 worth came from other countries and the balance from the United States; or, in other words, the United States had all the business. Against that business we are adding an additional half cent tax. Now we come to mutton. My hon. friend has referred to the importations of mutton from Australia. During that year we imported a total of $221,596 of mutton, and $193,426 of that came from the United States. Prom Australia we imported $13,527 worth and from New Zealand $5 801, and let me say that New Zealand is four days nearer to Canada than Australia. We imported from all other countries $8,842 worth. Now we come to pork, and incidentally let me say we import pork during slack seasons for use in our packing factories, and very often when this is exported as bacon 99 per cent of the duty is rebated, but it gives employment to Canadian workmen in the slack season.

Could you tell us how much we imported last year?
14011-227J

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We imported of fresh pork
for the year I am quoting now a total of $1,095,778 worth. Where do we import that from? None from Australia, none from New Zealand none from any country but the United States. It all comes from the United States and against that we are raising the tariff one-half cent a pound. My hon. friend who has been preaching politics throughout this session rises to-day to protest against this change.

I
do not like a statement of that kind to be made when it is not based on fact.
Mr. R'OBB:	Of all other meats we imported a total of $26,585 worth of which only $19 worth was from countries other than United States.
The minister will understand that I advocate increasing the tariff so as to make it equal to that of the United States against us instead of reducing or raising it by this amount, one-half cent.

speechtext: I cannot agree with that.

The minister says that he cannot agree with that. That is the reason why I was asking upon what principle they based the increase of one-half cent a pound. It is to enable the Australians and New Zealanders to have an advantage of three cents a pound in our market. While the minister has given the figures for last year he does not need to go very far back to find that some years seven or eight million pounds of Australian and New Zealand mutton were imported into Canada. It is true that not very much was imported last year until the Australian treaty went into effect.

What were the importations
of mutton from Australia prior to March 31, 1926, and what have they been since the Australian treaty went into effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: During March, 1925, we imported from Australia 17,074 pounds of mutton. In March, 1926, after this treaty was in force, wc imported 4,640 pounds.
Let me suggest that a much fairer comparison would be to give the imports for the year ended March 31, 1926, and for the first three months under the Australian treaty.

If the minister will look at the return which he tabled to-day he will get some more light on the subject. It is only half an hour since the minister tabled a return on this point showing importations

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The only item under consideration was fresh meats and that is what I was referring to.

I was quoting from the
return in regard to meat and meat products.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Meat products is not involved in this.

I understand that and
the House understands it. Going into details we find that of beef, fresh, chilled or frozen, there were imported from the United States 133,248 pounds of a value of $35,910 and from all other countries, $240 worth. Of imutton and lamb, fresh, chilled or frozen, we imported from the United States 1,072,134 pounds of a value of $229,361 and from all other countries-and this is where the great increase occurs-we imported 310,523 pounds.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Included in that is some from Argentina.

The statement does not
say whence it comes, but there is a marked increase in that item. Of pork, fresh, chilled or frozen, we imported from the United States 5,701,418 pounds of a value of $1,042,403. Practically all the importations of pork came from the United States. Hitherto, there has been against these importations a duty of three cents a pound. I suppose, following out its low tariff policy, this government would have maintained this duty of three cents a pound, but it was induced to change that by reason of a dicker with Australia and New Zealand, and the foundation of this part of the Australian treaty seems to be that we give Australia a clear preference of three cents a pound on beef, fresh, chilled or frozen, and on mutton and pork, in order to aceom-modiate Australia which gives us nothing We now propose to increase the duty against the products of the United States by one-half cent a pound. The idea is not to give the farmers of this country any additional protection ^gainst -the United States, although they will incidentally get an additional protection of one-half cent a pound, but to accommodate Australia. It is really to open the markets of the farmers of Canada to the people of Australia and not to afford any additional protection against goods coming from the United States.
	[
What the hon. member for South Oxford asks is that our tariff on importations of these products from the United States be materially increased. The demand from this side of the House and from the farmers in Canada in general is that they be protected against importations of these goods from the United States. If the minister had listened to the arguments addressed to this House from time to time by the hon. member from South Oxford, he could realize only one thing, namely, that the hon. member for South Oxford, who is a farmer himself, made his demand plain and insistent and we on this side do the same. This additional duty of one-half cent a pound is of no value whatever; it wi'l not check importations of United States beef, or mutton, or pork. I want to call the attention of the House, and especially of the minister,


Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
to an important fact. For a few years past the raising of sheep has been one industry in which the people of the western provinces have taken a great pride. There was a time years ago when Australian mutton was imported in such large quantities on the Pacific coast as almost completely to destroy the industry in the western provinces, and in order to revive and stimulate the raising of sheep the duty was increased so as to shut out that imported mutton. Under the tariff as proposed to-day, however, there is such a reduction as to encourage the revival of the Australian trade with the result that Australian mutton will flood the Canadian market. The minister has given us the imports during the past three years. While, in 192^, 139,000 pounds came into Canada and in 1925 and 1926, 117,000 and 215,000 pounds respectively, I would point out that according to a return which was brought down in the House and which I have in my hand there has been imported during the first six months in which the Australian treaty has been in force no less a quantity than 185,643 pounds of Australian mutton which has been sold on the Canadian market. I earnestly urge that something be done to maintain this great industry in western Canada. The west is better adapted to the raising of sheep than it is to any other branch of the live stock industry. What I predicted before has come to pass in western Canada, where we find to-day sheep being sold at from three to four dollars per head less than before this treaty came into effect. I am firmly of the opinion that if something is not done to offset the influence of that agreement this industry will be, if not ruined, at least seriously injured. In the interests of sheep raisers, not only in western Canada but throughout the Dominion, I therefore appeal to the minister to increase the tariff and so protect and build up the industry we now have.

I endorse what the hon.
member says concerning the precarious condition of the sheep industry in Canada to-day.
Our showing in this industry has 4 p.m. never at any time been flattering to Canadian farmers and to the Canadian people generally. We have in Canada two and three-quarter million sheep as compared with forty million in the United States and eighty million in Australia. Immediately after the war Australian mutton and lamb were shipped into the United States through the port of San Francisco, and Argentine mutton and lamb through the Atlantic ports, to such an extent as to create
alarm in the American industry. It was feared that these importations would destroy the industry there and without any waste of time the United States authorities increased their tariff with the result that the importations have been very considerably reduced, the home market being preserved to the American producers. The situation is quite serious from our point of view. The Australian and New Zealand sheep growers can produce both mutton and lamb cheaper than we can, indeed, cheaper than any other country is able to produce these commodities, and this is due largely to their favourable climatic conditions and to the fact that they can raise their stock on grass the year round. And when you consider this grave fact, that in years of drought in Australia and New Zealand mutton and lamb fall in price owing to the tendency to rush them on the foreign market before they become affected, there is a very great danger of these products being dumped in very large quantities on the Canadian market. Taking all these facts into consideration, therefore, I certainly think we ought to protect our sheep industry by means of larger tariffs both on mutton and lamb and on wool. We ought to frame our tariff to suit our own needs and should manage the affairs of this country to the best of our ability for the benefit of the Canadian people instead of being quite so generous with other countries.

I wish to support most heartily the remarks of the hon. member for East Calgary as well as those of the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie). There is a large district given over to sheep raising in my part of the country, and the people engaged in the industry there are very much worried about the present tariff proposed by the minister. There is however another matter I want to emphasize particularly and in connection with which I would ask the minister a question. Does the minister know whether the attention of his colleague the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) has been drawn to the fact that the hog cholera prevailing, in western Ontario in particular, is attributed to the importata-tion of American pork and that if that pork were kept out of the Canadian market there would be no fear of this disease in the various districts in which hogs are raised?

The minister having dealt with the matter, I assumed that I would be permitted to refer to his remarks. I ask, upon what grounds does the minister base the fixing of this item in the tariff? In other countries they have

tariff commissions. For instance, in the United States a short time ago the tariff commission took steps to ascertain the cost of production of butter in Denmark. They reported to the United States government that it was produced there for 12 cents a pound less than it cost to produce similar butter in the United States. Thereupon the president put the tariff up 12 cents a pound, or an increase of 50 per cent. The same thing happened with regard to wheat. The commission reported to their government that wheat could be produced in Canada for 42 cents a bushel less than it could be produced in the United States on account of the lower cost of land and the greater yield per acre in Canada. At once the duty against Canadian wheat was raised 42 cents a bushel.
Now, the minister would surely be well advised to ascertain the cost of producing meats in Australia, New Zealand, United States and in the Dominion. Does he contend that it is not possible to produce mutton and lamb in this country in sufficient quantities to supply the home demand? Is this country not producing all that is required along that line? If the minister takes that ground, I suppose it is some justification for his action, because while our friends opposite advocate free trade in relation to many things that can be and are produced in this country, yet they are strong protectionists when it comes to certain commodities that we do not produce. By way of illustration, let me point out that the tariff on tea is ten cents a pound. Does the minister think he is going to grow tea in this country? Here, however, is an item which we can produce in abundance and have a surplus for export. But there is always the danger of a tremendous importation of this commodity, just as happened this year in regard to butter. In that instance it will be remembered the government had to step in and apply the dumping clause because eight million pounds had been imported during the last few months. Their action, I contend, is absolutely unsound and not based on the principles underlying the dumping clause in the tariff. These are some of the anomalies in regard to our tariff, and I think the minister would be well advised to ascertain the cost of production of meat and meat products in this country as compared with the cost in the United States and other countries.
Let me point out, Mr. Chairman, that in other countries they do not call a tariff item "protection." My friends to the left rather imagine that every item in a tariff constitutes a certain degree of protection. The United States tariff commission refer to it

as follows: For example, the existing duty on a particular commodity does not equalize, as between the foreign and domestic manufacturer, the production costs ascertained as provided in the statute. Now, if those commodities can be produced in another country cheaper than in this country, is not that a sound argument for affording a corresponding degree of protection, particularly on an item such as this? Meats and meat products are things that this country can produce in abundance, but the government is doing nothing to encourage those engaged in raising live stock; in fact, it is not making the slightest attempt to redeem the promises contained in the Speech from the Throne to induce farmers to remain on the land and also to persuade those who have had training in agriculture but are now living in urban centres to go back to the land. Does the minister think he is carrying out those promises by removing the small degree of protection our farmers have?
There is a scheme on foot to give the farmers in this country what is termed rural credits. They are not asking for rural credits. Would

the hon. gentleman has just stated, may I say that the deputy minister was asked if it was possible for hog cholera to find entrance through the importation of dead meat. His reply was that it was quite possible, just as every farmer knows that it is.

As a member of the Sheepbreeders' Association of the province of Alberta, and being a sheepbreeder myself, I fully appreciate the importance of this industry. Let me say in that connection that the people of Canada through their respective governments have spent hundreds of thousands of dollars in developing the industry to its present stage. In every province the government have been spending money year after year buying the very best of stock and distributing it among the farmers with that object in view. I know of cases where the owners of herds of sheep-

speechtext: I direct your attention to what I am sure you already know, and what surely my genial friend the former Minister of Finance knows, that the amendment is out of order.
On what ground?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It increases taxation. However I am in the judgment of the committee.

Speaking to the point of order. I submit it is not necessarily an increase of taxation at all. You may raise the tariff, and you may not import the pork, and if there is no importation, there is no taxation whatever. Therefore I submit it is not necessarily an increase of taxation at all. If the amendment is not out of order on some other ground than that, then it is in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Sir Thomas Erskine
May, at page 462, says:
The principle that the sanction of the crown must be given to every grant of money drawn from the public revenue, applies equally to the taxation levied to provide that revenue. No motion can therefore be made to impose a tax, save by a minister of the crown, unless such tax be in substitution, by way of equivalent, for taxation at that moment submitted to the consideration of parliament; nor can the amount of tax proposed on behalf of the crown be augmented, nor any alteration made in the area of imposition. In 1'ke manner, no increase can be considered either of an existing, or of a new or temporary tax for the service of the year, except on the initiative of a minister, acting on behalf of the crown.
Then again May, at page 463, says:
So long as an existing tax is not increased, any modification of the proposed reduction may be introduced in the committee on the bill, and is regarded as a question, not for increasing the charge upon the people, but for determining to what extent such charge shall be reduced.
I therefore have to rule the amendment is out of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Now that we have got back to order again, may I just place on record the facts about the sheep industry of Canada and the injury to trade by importations. For the year 1926 we exported of mutton $593,475, and we imported $269,145; or in other words we exported almost double the quantity we imported. My hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) has referred to the duty imposed by the United States. He will be interested to know that out of our total exports of $593,475, $523,130 was exported to the United States.

With regard to the matter of importation of pork, I may say that it is generally accepted that hog cholera can be conveyed to other animals by the fresh, or even cured meat, of an infected hog. We have provided against that disease in Canada by quarantining live hogs for a period of about two months at the boundary line, making it impossible to import hogs for slaughter under those conditions, on account of the heavy cost of the quarantine. We have also recognized that fact in our garbage feeding regulations of the Department of Agriculture, whereby garbage feeders are compelled to cook all garbage very thoroughly before feeding, and we have other regulations in connection therewith.
With regard to the minister's remark concerning the period in which I was Minister of Agriculture, and my failure at that time to impose a tariff on American mutton or sheep, or to increase that tariff, let me say that I went into office late in 1919, and I went out after the earthquake in December 6, 1921. The hon. minister will no doubt

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
remember that during that period the American government were considering the increasing of their tariff on agricultural products, and at that time it would have been in my opinion very injudicious indeed for us to aggravate the situation by making any suggestion for an increased tariff on this side. I would like to point out to the minister that they have occupied the treasury benches since December, 1921, up to the present moment, and have done nothing in the way of giving the farmers and producers on the land of this country any increased protection.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Now when we are trying to give them that protection you stop us.
You now propose to take off the protection against the greatest sheep and lamb producing countries in the world, and put it on as against the United States.

I have before me now
chapter 30 of the statutes of Canada of 1925 giving the provisions in relation to the British preferential tariff concessions made by Australia to Canada and vice versa. It is true that in the schedule under tariff item 7, meats fresh n.o.p., the tariff rate is one-half cent a pound, but in the act of ratification and in the treaty itself it is provided as follows:
Provided that the proportionate difference between the rates set out opposite the items above enumerated in this schedule and the general tariff rates under the said items respectively shall at no time be less than it is at the time when the said above-mentioned rates come into force.
Under that provision it is very clear that this parliament, within the rights reserved under the treaty with Australia, can raise the tariff on importations on fresh meats from that country ito any rate per pound this parliament may in its discretion deem advisable, provided that the general tariff rate is raised proportionately or to exactly the same extent.

We suffer from several disadvantages at this end of the chamber. We do not as a rule hear what is going on; we miss many of the speeches, and we have great difficulty in catching the eye of the chairman. I am sure I have several times risen ahead of any other member, but I have failed to catch the chairman's eye. We have however to put up with those little disadvantages. It has been suggested that we have another chairman at this end of the chamber. So much has been said regarding the deplorable condition in which the sheep industry finds itself at present that I feel I must say a few words on the matter. I am not wholly a wheat farmer; I raise both

cattle and sheep. There is no part of the industrial life of the farm that is at the present time so profitable as sheep raising and I am going to give the House the exact figures as to the price I received for my lambs last year. I sold the lambs from their mothers, without their getting any other feed than they got from their mothers, and the grass they got, at $10.50 apiece. That means $21 from one ewe. The ewe got nothing but some straw and hay, costing almost a trifle, to bring her through the winter, and in the spring a little grain and the roughage she could pick up in the yard. Under such circumstances when you get $21 from one ewe in addition to the value of her fleece, I do not know of any other agricultural pursuit in the Dominion that pays as well as sheep raising. There are in connection with sheep raising some disadvantages to which I want my friends to the right to pay attention. One great disadvantage at present is the price of fencing, because there is a duty of 30 per cent on woven wire. I want the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) who is so anxious to help the sheep-raising industry to get woven wire fencing down to the lowest possible price.
Did the removal of the duty lower the cost of barbed wire? Did it not raise the price?

We will take a chance in
any case. In regard to wolves, all the wolves in Canada are not after the sheep. There is no doubt this is a serious drawback on the prairies in connection with sheep-raising and woven wire fencing with a mesh too small for wolves to get through would be of advantage so that sheep raisers would be greatly assisted if the price of wire fencing were reduced. On everything you sell the cost of production has a great deal to do with the profits likely to be made. As regards agriculture, our complaint is that everything we buy is too dear.

What is
the duty on wire fencing?

I cannot say exactly. I
think it is about 30 per cent. Some of my hon. friends would expect me to be a walking encyclopedia when I begin to speak, but I am not that. As farmers we have always claimed that we are able to compete with our products in the markets of the world and we are not complaining so much about the products regarding which my hon. friends are asking this afternoon. Anyone who has studied agricultural conditions knows that all the agricultural importations into Canada will not make much difference. President

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
Coolidge said the other day that within the lifetime of his hearers the United States would be the greatest agricultural importing country in the world. The United States does not balance its budget to-day on agriculture; it is importing instead of exporting so far as the balance is concerned. I know of course it exports meats, wheat and cotton, but the day is approaching very fast when those exportations will cease and that will be Canada's day. The Canadian agriculturist can compete with the farmer anywhere else in the world if he has a fair chance and is able to produce at the cost at which he ought to be able to produce. I want to tell my hon. friends that when they talk of benefiting agriculture they begin at the wrong end. I notice a tremendous difference between this parliament and the last one in this regard. In the last parliament the whole stress was on industry, but in this parliament there is a new move. The board of strategy must have been at work again and the whole idea to-day is to teach the farmer that he can be benefited by protection. I hope he will never fall for that.

I have listened to the
hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) and he is hardly fair when he makes any such statement as he made when he sat down, namely, that in the last parliament we were not interested in farming; that we were interested only in what he called industry. In the first place all people in this country admit that farming is the greatest industry of all; but even laying that aside, our whole attitude has been since I have been in this House-and I have been here for some ten years-to protect all classes of producers in Canada. This has not been any move of the so-called board of strategy-and I do not know where that name came from- but it is a move on the part of the Conservative party, in consistently living up to the policy of protection, to endeavour to build up all the different industries, the farming industry, the manufacturing industry and the industry of the labouring people of this country by a consistent policy of protection. Among his last words he quoted something from President Coolidge. I would suggest that he quote what Mr. Coolidge said a short time ago when he declared that the duty on butter should be increased from eight cents to twelve cents-while our duty against American butter was only four cents. Why *did President Coolidge make that statement? Simply because the farmers of the United States had asked him for protection against Canadian butter going into that country.
When therefore the hon. gentleman undertakes to quote President Coolidge he ought to quote him in full.
Hon. gentlemen opposite are inclined to charge us with playing politics when we speak in the interests of the Canadian farmer.
Hear, hear.

Hon. gentlemen say "hear, hear": evidently they judge us by themselves. I do not know how many farmers there are in this section of the House, and indeed I shall take the trouble some day to count them up. But I can say without the slightest hesitation that there are a large number of farmers in this party, gentlemen who have made a success of agriculture, who are just as vitally interested in the welfare of agriculture in Canada as are other hon. gentlemen who presume to speak on behalf of the farmers of Canada. Any man with ordinary intelligence-and I hope we are all intelligent enough to understand the facts-must believe that the good of the farmers is the good of Canada. We believe in protecting the farmers, whether they be sheep growers or any other class.
Now to come to the item under discussion. I have not taken the trouble to retain in my mind the figures which I have seen myself, but I am informed that Canada has .probably the smallest number of sheep of any agricultural country in the world. Someone says that Australia, for example, has at least forty times the number of sheep we raise in Canada; and more than that, the number here is steadily going down. I am not going to argue with the minister the necessity for increasing our duty on mutton and lamb coming into Canada from Australia, because apparently he has made up his mind that there shall be no changes in this regard, and no doubt he has enough support to carry out his intention. I will, however, argue this point with him. When the Australian treaty was first discussed the basis upon which it was con-5 p.m. sidered was the desire of Australia for higher duties on nearly every commodity which she might ship into Canada when those commodities come from other countries; and it was only after extended negotiations between the present minister (Mr. Robb) and the Australian government that it was decided to concede these low duties to the United States and other countries on many of the products which the Australian producers are exporting to this country. In short, they aimed at an increase to other countries in the duties on goods they wanted to sell to Canada, and it is obvious that Australia would be only

too glad to have our duty on mutton and lamb increased to other countries so long as it was reduced to Australian sheep raisers. I submit to the minister, therefore, that so far as this item is concerned he will only be carrying out his treaty agreement with Australia by shutting out a large proportion of mutton coming from the United States by imposing a protective tariff against that country. Such a duty against the United States would serve the double purpose of fulfilling the treaty with Australia-indeed, it would enhance the value of the treaty to that country-and, to some extent, of assisting the Canadian sheep industry in so far as it would protect our producers against the United States. What harm an increase in duty against United States producers could1 do to the raisers of sheep in Canada is something that passes my comprehension. It certainly could do nothing but improve the position of the industry in Canada. No matter what the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) may think of protection in general, I do not think he should have any objection whatever to the sheep growers, himself included, making a greater profit out of the industry by securing the home market.
The United States farmer has been deceived in the belief that protection would do something for him and I do not want the farmers in Canada to be deceived in the same way.

I do not want to be in
any way offensive to my hon. friend, but it seems to me that the hon. gentleman has the idea that the only farmers who have any intelligent grasp of fiscal matters come from Brandon and vicinity. I fancy that the farmers of the United States are sufficiently intelligent to understand their own interests, and they have consistently demanded of the United States President, and received from him, an increase in the tariff on agricultural products going into the United States from Canada.

The hon. member knows
very! iwell that agriculture in tha United States, especially in the northwest, is in a deplorable condition, and that the farmers are asking the government to take care of their surplus products.

That only adds force to
what I say: they want the United States government to protect them in every way. If the hon. member will look up the figures he will find that since the Fordney tariff went into force the exports from Canada to the United States in respect of a large number

of agricultural products have declined manyfold. Now, for the life of me I cannot understand the attitude of any farmer in Canada who feels that we should treat the American farmer or, for that matter, any producer in the United States, with any greater degree of consideration than they are prepared to show us. I think we should improve the sheep industry of this country in every possible way, and one means of doing so would be an increase in the duty on mutton and lamb coming from the United States, even if we leave the duty on imports coming from Australia at the figure which the minister proposes.
The argument is frequently put forward that unless you sell you cannot buy; there must be freedom of trade. How is it that some of the most highly protected countries in the world, such as Germany before the war, the United States to-day and France, if you will, keep on trading with other nations on such a large scale in face of the high protection they maintain? They keep on trading because they buy such lines of goods as they do not themselves produce, and export such goods as are not protected or produced in other countries. Trade is always going on between countries, and the fact that we may protect the sheep industry in this country is not going to stop our trading with the rest of the world.

Is my hon. friend
aware that our foreign trade per capita is three times that of the United States?

I do not know that that has anything to do with the question, inasmuch as what is of importance to any country is not the foreign trade but internal business, the ability of the people to buy and sell among themselves and to provide work and wages for their workers rather than force them to go to highly protected countries to seek a living.

I am nearly through anyway, Mr. Chairman. I saw many of my good friends from Saskatchewan, whose views are supposedly the quintessence of all that is in the interests of the farmers, waiting for an opportunity to differ from me. Let me make one more appeal to them; it is this. Let us

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
treat the United States, in relation to all branches of industry, including the raising of sheep and the production of mutton, lamb and wool, in the only way in which one self-respecting people should treat another. Let us adopt the honourable and the proud principle of doing unto them as they do unto us, and we shall secure their respect. The only principle on which we shall ever be able to transact business with them to our own satisfaction is to deal with -them in a strictly businesslike way.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am very glad, Mr. Chairman, that you directed our attention to the fact that this is not a second budget debate, nor is tire Australian treaty under consideration. They say a woman has the right to change her mind occasionally and perhaps a member of parliament also has that right. I recall that the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) was one of those who came to. my room urging that this Australian treaty be proceeded with. Some of the gentlemen who came canvassing me to put this agreement through will have to take the responsibility if Australia cancels an agreement which has been very profitable to this country.
Would the minister inform us in what way it has been profitable to Canada? Has not the favourable balance of trade decreased?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have increased our trade
enormously, and the farmers who supply , the foodstuffs for the men working in the paper mills, and those men as well, all receive additional benefits. The hon. member for Fort William not only urged me to put this treaty through when there was some doubt whether it would be proceeded with, but he was one of those who loyally stood up and voted for it. To-day he attempts to delay the passing of an item which is designed to carry out that agreement.

I ask the privilege of
replying for a moment or two. The minister has implied that I was inconsistent this afternoon in relation to what I said last year.
I do not think I have shown any inconsistency; no man either in or out of this House ever heard me attack the Australian treaty, in which attitude I am at some difference with hon. members around me. But I would like my hon. friend to be fair; I said this afternoon that he could do something to enhance the value of this treaty to the Australian people by raising the duty on sheep and mutton coming from the United States. I do not criticize anything he said about my having been one of those who asked him to put this treaty through. As a matter of fact I gave my reasons for so doing last year; if I had Hansard I could read my own words, but I said that I thought the Australian treaty was in some ways bad for the farmers of this country. At the same time, since northern Ontario was a large producer of pulp and paper; since I represent a constituency in that part of the province, and since the pulp and paper interests were deriving some benefit from this treaty, I must take the lesser of the two evils. But it will also appear in Hansard that I said then that if we got back into power, as I thought we were going to after the last election-
Hear, hear.

We did virtually get into power, although we do not now have the reins of power. My good friend the Minister of Finance and his confreres are too fond of power to give it up so long as they can get a group of any kind to support them. 1 want to point out that in making that statement last year I said that the first thing I would advocate if we got into power would be a general, all round increase of the tariff on agricultural products from every other country of the world. So I was absolutely consistent, and if the Minister of Finance thinks he is frightening me at all by threatening that Australia will cancel the treaty, he has another thought coming to him. I am not so easily frightened as all that; it is up to the people of Australia. My argument is that we can enhance the value of this treaty to the Australian people and improve conditions in this country as well by treating other countries as they have treated us.

I only rise because of the remarks of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke). I would like to tell him that there were men in this House advocating the cause of the farmers and workmen of this

No, Mr. Chairman. A short time ago I asked a question of the Minister of Finance in regard to this item. Perhaps he did not intend to evade the question, but he certainly did not answer it. That does seem to me to be a good reason why the general tariff of 3J cents should be raised. I do not suppose that Australia or New Zealand will object to a greater preference than three cents per pound. There is another board, of which I believe he is chairman, that is a sort of supplement to the cabinet. It is my privilege, of course, to ask a question which I conceive to have a very direct bearing upon the item under discussion ,and it is the minister's privilege to answer or not, as he sees fit.
I say that the question I asked had a very direct bearing for this reason. We are discussing item 7, and the minister himself said that the rate of three and one-half cents per pound was fixed because of the agreement with Australia. Australia having a rate of one-half cent per pound and the agreement requiring that Australia be given a preference of three cents, the minister fixes the rate at three and one-half cents per pound. In bringing meat into Canada from any other country there are certain factors entering into that transaction; there is the duty, the cost of transportation, and still another matter which has been recognized by this government. In some countries, one at least, the government or certain societies undertake to encourage the transportation or exportation of certain goods by giving a bonus. For example-and this I submit to be a fair illustration-the duty on butter coming from a certain country was fixed at one cent per pound. In the course of time it developed that by an arrangement in that country called the Pattersen scheme a bonus of six cents was given on every pound of butter exported. We have been told repeatedly that the government did consider that as a factor which influenced the agreement entered into, and I understand they are applying a dumping clause of six cents per pound because of the action of this society.
Now I make the application to meats. The government of Australia gives a bonus, I am told, of $2.40 on every carcass of beef exported from that country. Although the amounts are different that is on all fours with the Pattersen scheme of bonusing butter, and if the government recognize one scheme as militating against Canada and unfair to the dairymen, then I ask why the same thing should not be taken into consideration in regard to meats. The $2.40 paid by the Australian government on every carcass of beef exported will, I presume, work out in the neighbourhood of one-half cent bonus per pound, so as a matter of fact, because of the bonus on the export of beef from Australia, there is really no protection at all. that bonus offsetting the duty of one-half cent per pound and leaving as our only protection the cost of transportation. Having in view the fact that this bonus is given, would it not be fair for the minister to

I do not think hon. members from British Columbia or the prairies need concern themselves much about any discrimination. In my opinion the whole scheme is impracticable. Notwithstanding this arrangement, I believe that 90 per cent of our bananas will still come from the United States, and in that case this is merely a tariff for revenue. I have letters from dealers in many parts of Ontario and also from Manitoba and the west in -which they express the opinion that it is utterly impossible for them to consider bringing in bananas through Canadian ports. The entire distribution of bananas i3 scientifically arranged by the three large companies engaged in the business. They are distributed from New Orleans, Baltimore, New York, Philadelphia and Boston, and every centre is reached within eight days. Let me give a few figures of comparative distances. The estimated distance direct from Kingston, Jamaica, to Halifax, is 1,834 nautical miles. The 14 knot passenger service which is provided for in the West India treaty would cover this distance in 138 hours; from Halifax to central Ontario points you have to allow another 120 hours; extra time for stops at the Bahamas and Bermuda would consume a further 24 hours-in all 282 hours, or 111 days. If the bananas are distributed from Montreal we would have to add one day to this time, for the simpile reason that the water trip from Halifax to Montreal would be just that much longer than the rail haul. The distance from Kingston, Jamaica, by the freight sendee, which is every other week, would take one day longer. The distance from Kingston, Jamaica, to Baltimore, New York and Philadelphia is given as 1,440 nautical miles, that would mean 103 hours, and the rail journey to central Ontario points would take 48 hours, making in all 151 hours. In other words, 6 days and 7 hours against a possible 121 to 13 days via Canadian ports. New Orleans and Mobile receive their supplies altogether from Central America, and in no case is the time over eight days from the point of shipment in Central America to our markets. This alone makes a difference of anywhere from three to five days. In addition, the dealers have the option of buying their bananas from every one of the ports mentioned every day of the week; they do not have to wait for their supplies. Take a firm handling three cars of bananas a week which many of our Ontario and Quebec firms do; they would have to buy them all at one time. Does the minister know that bananas cannot be held for an indefinite time 
for the simple reason that they cannot be kept in cold storage or in a temperature below 50 degrees for any length of time without becoming useless? On the other hand, in hot weather bananas can be held for only a very few days or they will become over-ripe.
For that reason we have the trade throughout the whole Dominion buying their supplies from ports not more than three, four or five days distant from the source of supply. Any day of the week they can get their bananas delivered, for instance, on Mondays, Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Thursdays and Fridays. I think the House will see how impracticable the scheme will be in view of the present distribution.
There is another thing I should like to point out to the minister. Why are the large importing companies who are looking for business all the time-there are three or four of them, but three anyway-not distributing from Montreal and Halifax now? If it were feasible to do so I know that those companies would be moving bananas from those ports now. These companies can still bring bananas to Canadian ports direct. If another service is inaugurated there is no reason why the existing companies cannot come up the St. Lawrence with their bananas and enjoy the benefit of the free entry. That would practically ruin any opposition that might be attempted. In my opinion all these matters are worth considering. I look upon this as one of
the most important things we are going to deal with in connection with the tariff. We have to-day in the Dominion two big sugar refineries which are only producing ten per cent of the sugar consumed in Canada. Now, if there is one industry that should be taken care of and protected it is the sugar industry. Last year there was a sugar factory built in the town of Raymond, Alberta, which has been very successful. While last year there were only eight thousand acres under cultivation, this year ten thousand acres are being cultivated. The seed for the production of the sugar beet is brought into Canada from Germany. To produce all the sugar used in Canada which could be produced from sugar beet we could have under cultivation
300.000	acres of land, giving employment to
100.000	people. To transfer that into sugar

In Alberta we have 1,000,000 acres of irrigated land, and I suggest that there is no place in the Dominion where sugar beets can be grown more successfully than in that province. The average yield per acre from the sugar beet is about 2,200 pounds of sugar. If there is a bright spot in Canada for development it is in connection with the sugar industry, and seed can be produced in British Columbia of an equal quality	with	any seed that	has	everbeen shipped	from	Germany. It	will	takethree-quarters of a million dollars' worth of seed to produce the sugar in quantities sufficient for	home	consumption. I leavethese thoughts with the government for their consideration	when	making treaties.	Let
them consider what a great advantage that would be to Canada as a whole and what an enormous amount of employment it would give. In order to make it a huge success and to make the business profitable, the industry must, in common with all other industries, be protected to some extent. All I ask is that the government give a kindly hearing to these representations and endeavour to stimulate that industry in which such a great amount of labour can be employed. W7e have a splendid foundation for such an industry in Canada, and taking it all in all I think Canada has a great future before it in the development of this industry.

I notice that all these figures

speechtext: No, these are the rates.

It seems to me absurd that we should have negotiated a treaty with the British West Indies, asking from them certain reductions and preferences in view of this parliament making certain reductions in the tariff and giving certain preferences to the West Indies, and yet before the West India treaty is ratified we re-enact a rate of duty which takes from the government all power of future negotiation with respect to the matter. This is resolution number 2, and schedule A is in resolution number 2. Resolution number 5 enacts:
That any enactment founded on the foregoing resolutions number two and three shall be deemed to have come into force on the sixteenth day of April, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-six, and to have applied to all goods mentioned in the foregoing resolutions imported or taken out of warehouse for consumption on and after that day, and to have applied to goods previously imported for which no entry for consumption was made before that day.
So that now, with the West India treaty negotiated but not yet ratified, in respect to which the government have not presented the detailed information to the House which was promised as soon as certain tenders for steamships were received, the minister comes to the House and asks us by statute to enact that since the 16th day of April 1926, these reductions have actually been made which were the consideration offered by the government for certain tariff considerations to be granted by the West Indies. In other words, before the treaty is ratified we are now giving to the British West Indies, without any consideration having been offered by them in the way of tariff reductions, a free gift which takes away from the government all power of negotiation.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend, who is an
old experienced parliamentarian and who has been following the business of parliament for many years, will remember that in 1921, when the party he now supports made a treaty with the West India Islands, they adopted the same process and procedure.
Before the treaty had been negotiated?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: After the treaty was negotiated, and it came into force the day the minister presented his budget. That is the way it is generally done. The hon. member says we are giving to the West Indies a gift or an additional concession. We are doing nothing of the kind. We are giving an additional concession-I will admit that at once -to the West India planter and to the Canadian sugar refiner. The Canadian sugar refiner will get a part of this benefit.
In what respect?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Because there is an additional something over 16 cents a hundred in their favour. I imagine they will divide it between them. Let me point this out to my hon. friend and to my friend from the west. When the West India delegates were in Canada they were most insistent that we should give them some additional advantages in their gray sugars. They wanted to get their grays into this market. We said: No, we must look after Canadian interests and the Canadian refiners. We had in mind the beet industries that were started throughout Canada and the Canadian refining industry that employs labour. We insisted on that, but I am not so sure to-day whether we were quite wise or not. I notice in the press of the United States that there is a good deal of criticism of the protection given to the refiners of that country, and I have noticed some of the same

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
criticism in Canada. It is true there is not much to-day because sugar is fairly cheap; the raw sugar is cheap and consequently the refined is down in price. But if the price of sugar became high again we might find an agitation throughout this country for a little cheaper sugar for the Canadian people, so that I think we are dealing fairly well with the trade generally and with the West India planter.

I do not understand that
a preference given to the West Indies is >f very much advantage to the Canadian sugar refiner, because the Canadian refiner of imported raw sugar will certainly charge up again to the Canadian consumer whatever duty he pays on the raw article. But this is the point I wish to' make: We have negotiated a treaty with the West Indies; that treaty has been submitted to the consideration of this House and it is not yet ratified. In the treaty there appear certain provisions with regard to steamship subsidies and the employment of steamships. 'The Minister of Finance stated before the long adjournment that at the close of that adjournment he hoped to be in a position to place before the House the result of the tenders then being received so that the House would be in a position to decide definitely whether or not it would ratify the West India treaty as a whole. But before that treaty, which provides for certain preferences on the sugar tariff in favour of the West Indies, has been finally ratified by the House the minister presents to us resolutions granting to the West Indies every preference which the West Indies would have had if the treaty itself had been ratified. I ask the minister if he is not thereby throwing away every consideration which he offered to the West 'India delegates as grounds for their making corresponding concessions to Canada. He says: This is the ordinary practice of the House and the practice which was followed when the previous West India treaty was brought before the House by the previous government. I suggest to the minister that when the reductions were made in the general tariff on the previous occasion the West India treaty had been ratified by parliament, and these tariff amendments were made in order to conform to the treaty which had been ratified. It seems to me, with all deference, that the Minister of Finance, if I may use the expression, is now placing the cart before the horse. Before the treaty is ratified, before he is in a position to place before the House the material and salient facts which will be grounds for ratification of that treaty, we have resolutions introduced

which grant all those concessions and which under the terms of the fifth resolution come into full force and effect on the 16th day of April, 1926.
In order to deal fairly with the public interests of this country I suggest to the minister that we should in these resolutions take power in the government to make the reductions which are here made, but that the reductions so made should come into force only by authority of an order in council to be passed when the corresponding treaty with the British West Indies comes into full force and operation. I am suggesting that as being fair to the House and to the country and conserving the interests of all parties.
I do not think no attention should be paid to the remarks of the hon. member.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was waiting to see if other
hon. gentlemen had observations to make.

It would be a
good thing to get rid of this question; it is the same as I have suggested with regard to the cocoa item. These are treaty items and the treaty is not yet ratified. There are some difficulties in connection with the treaty and my hon. friend has recognized them. He has recognized in connection with bananas that the matter cannot become law now. He keeps his hand on it; he is going to police it. T! e change in the duty on bananas does not come into effect now; it will come into effect only when the government takes action. All that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George is suggesting is that precisely the same thing shall be done in connection with sugar as has been done in connection with bananas. It s done in connection with bananas simply because there is the contingency not only . that the treaty may not be ratified but that there may be difficulties in regard to supplying the service. But the fact that the difficulty is greater in connection with bananas than in connection with sugar is no reason why the same course should not be followed in connection with both. If my hon. friend will arrange when the bill comes down to have a provision inserted that the change will come into effect only when the appropriate order in council is passed after the agreement is ratified, that is the easiest thing to do. If my hon. friend says he will do it, the thing is settled at once.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am following the procedure which my hon. friend followed in 1921. I have under my hand a memorandum sent out to the collectors of customs and excise indicating that the West India rates have

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
been brought into effect prior to the ratification of the treaty. Regarding the observations of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, I hold the position again that this is a concession to the Canadian people as well as to the West India planter. They may divide it between them, but this additional concession on the raws cannot 'all go to the planter. If later for any reason the AVest India agreement is not put through, there will be nothing to hinder us in another parliament from correspondingly reducing the duty on refined sugars. Does my hon. friend favour a reduction in refined sugars corresponding to the reduction in the raws?

If there is a reduction in raw sugar and no corresponding reduction in refined sugar you give a greater protection to the refiners than they had before. It all depends upon the disclosures of an investigation as to whether the refiners are getting sufficient protection or too much, whether they are profiteering or not. What I say is this: In order to negotiate with the British West Indies we need to keep up the tariff on raw sugars. For my part I would keep them up on refined sugars to a corresponding extent so as to give adequate protection to the Canadian refiners. The minister by proposing to put the reduction in raw sugars into force from a specified date, is giving to the West Indies, without any consideration in return, a concession which he previously reserved as a ground on which to negotiate a treaty which he commends to the House for support. That is impolitic and it is unbusinesslike. I suggest that he reconsider that decision, because, in my opinion at least, when the bill comes before the House for discussion we should protest the manner in which the minister is carrying out these reductions before the treaty has been ratified by parliament. In the bill he might very well consider the advisability of bringing this provision into operation by order in council after the treaty has been ratified. If that treaty were not ratified I for one would not endorse the reductions at all. I am simply supporting them, if I do support them, on the ground that they are concessions given in a treaty with the West Indies in return for which we are to receive certain equivalent values. On that ground I am prepared to consider favourably the items suggested in the West India treaty. On the other hand the minister recognizes, I am sure, as well as does the hon. member for East Lambton, that in making these reductions on raw sugar he is taking away from the beet sugar industry of this country a large part of the
protection which it now has. He is in effect, without any inquiry or even any suggestion of an inquiry, reducing the protection which has been allowed to the cultivation of beets in Canada, and he will destroy to a very large extent, I believe, and certainly will prejudice very seriously the Canadian producers of beet-root. There is no doubt, from the knowledge and experience we have, that beets can be grown in the province of Quebec in sufficient quantities to supply a large part of the sugar needed for consumption in that province. We all know, too, that Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia are in large part as well adapted to the growing of beets and the production of beet sugar as are Germany, Belgium and northern France, and there is no reason in the world why we should not, so far as we possibly can, safeguard and foster that growing industry, looking to the future.
To sum up, therefore: my objection is that by statute the minister is now reducing the tariff, the reductions to come into
10	p.m. force from a specified date, when they should be made effective only upon ratification of the treaty. He should reserve the power to make the reductions by order in council, contingent upon the treaty with the West Indies being ratified. In any case, in my point of view, he should put up the duty even higher on raw sugar, giving a preference to the West Indies and at the same time retaining adequate protection for this growing industry in Canada.

the industry for twelve years under this agreement. For that length of time the spread now proposed will be maintained. As regards making changes in the bill, I will consider the matter overnight, although I should prefer to follow the procedure of the former Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) and put it through. speechtext:
Well, admitting that we were
all in it-
Yes, admit that.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -there has been a delay, just the same. The West Indies carried out their part of the bargain, putting through the necessary legislation so far as they were concerned. I do not know whether my hon. friend was in the House when I told hon. members that representations had been made to us that certain people were prepared to put on a steamer service between Canada and the West Indies. We want therefore to be in a position to enjoy the benefits of the trade at the earliest possible moment.

I want to repudiate one suggestion. The minister as a man of honour will admit that he has never yet been in a position to submit to the House the actual facts necessary to enable the House to form an opinion, either favourable or unfavourable, upon the West India treaty. Long ago the minister admitted that he had delayed asking for tenders so long that, as a matter of fact, the returns had not yet come in, so that he was unable to give us any details whatever as to the cost of the proposed service. It is therefore entirely his own fault that nothing has been done in the matter. Whether it was himself or someone else that did so I cannot remember, but a member sought to excuse the government on the ground that they had been so taken up with the elections in September and October as to have had no opportunity for calling for tenders and placing the facts before the country. I therefore take no responsibility for any delay. Personally I do not wish to press the matter. I am not sufficiently informed as to the 
practices that have formerly obtained, but I am free to admit that in my opinion there have been many bad practices which should be avoided by future governments, and this is one. We should not reduce our general tariff to correspond with preferential treaties before those preferential treaties are in force.

I had to tell
my hon. friend the other day that it was a matter of astonishment to me that he is so keen on following form and leaving out substance; he follows the letter but always forgets the principle. If he would only follow the principle of former administrations we would not have to say anything at all to him; he would be right. However, my hon. friend says that he will consider the matter and see what can be done, so I will say no more at present. But I would like to ask my hon. friend the reason for the changes in the schedule, apart from those changes necessitated by the West India treaty?

the British Board of Customs and Excise, which enables them to keep their records correct. They have a preference in the United Kingdom as well.

speechtext:

uniform, to correspond with the others.

speechtext:
The error might have been
greater before; that is the only explanation I have in mind.

explanation which cannot explain. You will find the same condition where you have rectified it.

work back.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understand it was simply
made to conform with the British practice. I am bound to say that it was beyond me to understand those experts when they were figuring it out.

My hon. friend will see that when we had a higher degree of protection our sugar beet growers were much better looked after. I am delighted to see one thing, however; my hon. friend to-day is a convert to the ideas of his predecessors as to the necessity of stability. He said today that this is a great thing for the growers of sugar beets in Canada, because they will now know that for twelve years they are to have stability. So I take it that he is now a convert to what Mr. Fielding told us a few years ago as to the necessity of tariff stability.

come in?
Because a contract has been made with the West Indies which is to run for twelve years.

this government from reducing the tariff still more in favour of the West Indies.

N.o, but the
minister says there will be stability now, because that contract runs for twelve years.
