tariff will be maintained, and that is what is undermining confidence among the people. Let us have some degree of stability. The minister has shown no regard whatever for the sugar beet industry; apparently it makes no difference to him whether we use sugar produced in Canada or sugar made by foreign labour. He thinks he has done enough when he comes to parliament and declares that he is going to provide rural credits legislation to relieve farmers who may be hard up. Surely this is not the principle upon which a sound policy should be based. I have endeavoured time and again to-day to induce the minister to state to the committee precisely on what principle these reductions are based, and what the government's objective is in its tariff legislation. The country is entitled to know just what the government proposes to do. It must have some assurance of tariff stability.

Knowing the minister as I do, I have been very, much surprised to hear the reasons he hag advanced for having been driven to this, that and the other change, but the surprise of the whole evening has been to hear him make the statement that this item had for its object the providing of lights on farms as a means of keeping the farmers' children at home. Bright lights will do the trick. As one who was brought up on a farm, I must say that I have listened to that sort of reasoning so much that I am about sick of it. The idea is preposterous that it was the bright lights of the city or any thing of that kind that attracted me and hundreds and thousands of others from the farm. It is absolute rot. The sons and daughters of farmers have as much brains as the sons and daughters of city people, and if they have taken advantage of their talents and their opportunities to go into other lines of business they have done so because they could not prosper on the farm. Now the farmer, along with other creatures he raises on his farm, rears more children than he can make use of, and many of them consequently are obliged to leave the farm. The minister proposes to retain these people by providing them with bright lights. That is not the idea at all; these are no reasons for the townward trend that has gone on for years. But I will tell you one reason. Agricultural development has taken place in the last sixty or seventy years and there has been a demand for those implements which have made farm work easier. These have been made in the cities and towns, and the farmers' boys in a large way assist in the manufacture of these implements. That is one reason for the townward trend, and it is not because of this lack of bright lights on

the farm, and all that sort of thing. Consequently I want to draw the attention of the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan) to the fact that if he has a boy on the farm and that boy is a mechanical genius, where is he to apply himself? My hon. friend is going to insist that that boy go to the United States, where thousands have gone for that very reason. We should recognize the fact that these batteries and so on can be made in Canada, and boys from our farms can get employment in these factories instead of going to the United States.

Does the hon.
member think he can keep that boy on the farm by keeping him in darkness?

If a boy has brains he will use them, whether or not you keep him in darkness. Do not keep him there if he has brains; give him a chance to get ahead, but give him a chance in Canada. We are not only sending our natural resources out of this country, but we are sending after them our most valuable natural resource, our boys and o-irls. Now I want to draw to the attention of the minister the fact that batteries are being made in Canada; men are just beginning to manufacture this electrical equipment, but they are becoming downhearted as they see one thing after another put through this House of Commons to give them less and less opportunity. I have listened to all these ways of keeping the boy on the farm, and I do not believe the minister believes in his heart one word of what he said. I know him well, and it is only trash and nonsense to say that this is going to keep the boy on the farm.

I have listened to the remarks made in reference to keeping the boy on the farm. When we who live in the country come to the city we recognize the tremendous advantages of city life) 'over country life in the matter of many conveniences. Eight is one, postal service another, and I think our city friends should be very anxious to help those on the farms enjoy some of the conveniences and luxuries ^ of modem civilization. Good light is something which will help keep the boy on the farm. Anyone who has ever lived in the country and who knows what the coal oil lamp means will know how difficult it is to enjoy reading on a winter evening with poor light. They will realize how good light makes country life more attractive. Perhaps I will not be in order, but I would like to give the reason why the boys are leaving the farm. The last speaker said we should not keep the boys on the farm if they had ability for other work, and I quite 14011-230

To go to the United
States.

No, Sir; their parents have
lived under great disadvantages and difficulties, and the children have grown up to appreciate this fact. We a,re proud of the fact that education is within the reach of every boy and girl. They go to the common schools, the high schools and the universities and have been educated away from the farm-not because education has done that, but they have learned the disadvantages of agricultural life and will not go back to the farm. I must be careful in what I say, because some people will think I am speaking against education. Education will not take a boy away from a farm if conditions on the farm are Tight. The way to keep the boys and girls on the farm is to make farm life so attractive that the cities will not draw them away. Light, while it may seem trivial, is very important.
I know what it is to sit through a long winter evening trying to read with a poor light, and I know that good light is a prime requisite. We simply ask that electric lighting plants for farms be made and sold as cheaply as they possible can. I would like to repeat what I said in opening; when I come to the city and realize the advantages of electric light,, almost like daylight, and consider the conditions on the average country farm, I think we should be prepared to do something to help those farmers get the very best light possible at the cheapest rates.

Mr. Chairman,

Within the last few days I met a gentleman who has travelled a good deal both in the United States and in Canada, and he said to me-I have seen something similar in the press-that the greatest advance in economics in the world to-day has been made by the western farmers in pooling their grain and taking over the selling of it, by which they have increased their price. Mr. Chairman, I did not

I cannot help thinking that if the hon. member for South Oxford would only analyze his own statements he would see how contradictory they are. He says that the genius and industry of our workmen are equal to those of any other workmen in the whole world, and that we can make electric lighting equipment here the equal to anything made in the whole universe. that equipment is worth less than the material and labour that went into its construction. If it was not so its manufacturers would not need protection. The very idea underlying the need of protection is that the value of the finished article is worth less than the raw material that entered into it. Nobody can deny that. It is an economic law. If it was, as the hon. member says, equal to any similar equipment made in the world it could be sold on its own merits. But there is not a thing that our manufacturers and workmen can touch to-day that would be worth as much finished as in the raw state, according to their plea for protection. That is the strange thing. Mostly.

The hon. member has even

We would give protection
all round.

The two-facedness of the

He has been advocating that

The principle underlying protection is that an industry cannot live and sell its product in competition with the world. How, then, can the farmer pay a high duty on what he needs, amounting in some cases to 35 per cent or more, and then sell his product against all the cheap labour of the whole world? We have to compete against Russia and India, where the people work for a few kopeks or a few annas a day. Is it reasonable, is it fair? Have our people lost all sense of right and British justice and fair play? Why, the thing has become too childish for words.

Mr. Chairman, I have been listening the whole evening and rather enjoy-14011-2301

I always notice that what he lacks in logic he supplies in enthusiasm. I say that with no disrespect, for I have the friendliest feeling for him. I have kept away from the discussion to-night because I thought someone would get up and say exactly what my hon. friend has said. But as a matter of fact the hon. member for South Oxford is absolutely consistent, and he showed his breadth of mind this afternoon by fighting for protection for the farmers and then standing up courageously to fight for protection for the other industries of this country, al-thought a farmer himself. Now, I do not pretend to any originality, but I certainly do believe that the people of Canada can protect all classes in this country, with the possible exception- and I have said it many times-of the wheat grower, who has to sell his product in the markets of the world. But the farmers in Ontario and Quebec-and there are two millions of them in these provinces, or about four times as many as there are in the prairie provinces-sell their products to the industrial centres in their neighbourhood to the extent of about ninety per cent.

speechtext: Yes. I agreed to leave certain items for consideration when the leader of the opposition was here.
When may we expect to take these items up again?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
To-morrow.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King, the House adjourned at 11.45 p.m.
Friday, May 21, 1926
